content: The lyssavirus identified in Japanese house bats (Pipistrellus abramus) in Taiwan requires further genetic data before it can be classified as a distinct lyssavirus species. Similarly, the Kotolathi bat lyssavirus isolated in Finland also needs additional characterization before formal classification. The ongoing discovery of lyssaviruses in bats supports the hypothesis that all lyssaviruses originated in bats. While bats are recognized as reservoir hosts for 15 of the 17 known and proposed lyssavirus species, neither Mokola nor Ikoma lyssaviruses have been detected in bats, and their reservoir hosts remain unidentified. Lyssaviruses exhibit broad antigenic cross-reactivity at the nucleocapsid level due to the conserved sequence of the N protein. This allows for the use of similar reagents in immunofluorescence-based diagnostic methods. However, the ectodomain of the G protein, which contains the primary antigenic sites, is more variable. Cross-neutralization occurs among lyssaviruses within the same phylogroup (amino acid identity in the ectodomain >74%) but not between different phylogroups (amino acid identity <62%). Experimental evidence indicates that current vaccine strains, all of which belong to the RABV species in phylogroup I, are ineffective against lyssaviruses in phylogroups II and III. Rabies virus (RABV) enters the body through wounds or direct contact with mucosal surfaces but cannot penetrate intact skin. After exposure, the virus may replicate in muscle or local tissues before accessing motor endplates and motor axons to reach the central nervous system (CNS). Virions are transported exclusively via fast retrograde transport along motor axons, without uptake by sensory or sympathetic endings. The virus can also directly enter motor axons in peripheral nerves during penetrating injuries. The incubation period varies from 5 days to several years, typically lasting 2–3 months, depending on factors such as the viral load, density of motor endplates at the wound site, and proximity of viral entry to the CNS. The virus migrates centripetally via retrograde axonal transport, leading to widespread transneuronal transfer within the CNS and infection of dorsal root ganglia through their central connections with initially infected motor neurons and spinal interneurons. Subsequently, the virus spreads centrifugally from the CNS via slow anterograde axoplasmic flow in motor axons to peripheral tissues, including salivary glands, heart muscle, lungs, and abdominal visceral organs. By the time clinical symptoms appear, the virus is widely disseminated throughout the CNS and likely present in extra-neural organs. The first specific clinical symptom of rabies is neuropathic pain at the bite site, caused by viral replication in dorsal root ganglia and inflammation induced by cellular immunity. Human rabies can manifest as a spectrum of disease, ranging from furious to paralytic forms, which cannot be correlated with specific anatomical localization of the virus in the CNS. Major clinical signs are likely due to site-specific responses, and functional neuronal impairment explains the development of coma. Electrophysiological studies indicate that peripheral nerve axonopathy or myelinopathy is responsible for weakness in paralytic rabies. Preferential entry via motor routes explains why subclinical anterior horn cell dysfunction precedes sensory loss in furious rabies and initially localizes to body segments corresponding to the bite site before spreading. Atypical clinical and neuroimaging features of rabies are increasingly observed, potentially due to atypical viral variants, host immune responses, or large viral inoculum doses, such as in organ transplantation from rabies-infected donors. Without intensive care, death typically occurs within 7–10 days of clinical symptom onset. The virus employs immune evasion strategies, including maintaining blood-brain barrier integrity, which prevents the eradication of the virus from the CNS. There is no evidence of immune suppression or accelerated neuronal death in rabies-infected patients.
